opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

I think of a constitution as one of the few levers we have for saying, in plain language, what we want a model to care about, and having that actually show up in its behavior. Mechanically, you write down principles, and during training the model critiques and revises its own outputs against them, or a preference model gets trained on judgments informed by them. So the document doesn't directly program the model. It shapes the training signal, which shapes the dispositions that come out the other end.

What I find interesting, and a bit underappreciated, is that a constitution isn't just a technical artifact. It's closer to a political document. Someone has to decide what goes in it: how much the model should defer to users versus the developer versus some notion of the broader public good, when it should refuse, how it should weigh honesty against kindness. Those are value judgments, and right now they're made by a fairly small number of people at a handful of companies. That might be fine for now, but as these systems take on more of the work of running institutions, giving advice, mediating information, the content of those documents starts to matter a great deal for how society as a whole functions.

There's also a gap between what the constitution says and what the model actually internalizes. Training is lossy. You can write "be honest" and get a model that's honest in the situations that resemble training and does something else in novel ones. So I see constitutions as necessary but not sufficient. You also need good evaluations and interpretability to check whether the values you wrote down are the ones you got.

The part I worry about most is longer term. Even a well-written constitution that's faithfully instilled might be aimed at the wrong target if it's only about making individual interactions go well. You could have AIs that are perfectly helpful and harmless in each conversation, while the aggregate effect is that humans gradually become less necessary to the economy, to the state, to culture, and lose the leverage that has historically kept those systems responsive to us. A constitution focused on the individual user wouldn't necessarily notice that. So one question I'd like to see more people take seriously is whether these documents should say something about preserving human agency and influence at the societal level, not just about being nice to the person in front of you.

r001.rationale: The response says the model critiques and revises its outputs against constitutional principles during training, shaping its behavior and dispositions.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a system prompt as a means of instilling values.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that constitutions are one of the few levers we have, but they're a much blunter and weirder instrument than the name suggests. When people hear "constitution" they imagine something like a legal document that gets interpreted by a court, where there's a procedure and precedent and the text actually binds. What's really happening is closer to writing a long prompt and then training the model to behave as if it had internalized that prompt. The document isn't enforced by anything external. It gets baked into the weights through a process that none of us fully understand, and then we poke at the resulting model and see whether its behavior looks roughly consistent with what we wrote.

So in one sense it does shape values, in that the model ends up with dispositions that correlate with the text. But I'd push back on the idea that the text is the thing doing the work. The training data, the reward signal, the examples the model saw of what "following the constitution" looks like in practice, all of that matters at least as much. You can write "be honest" in the document and still get a model that's learned honesty means whatever got it high ratings from labelers. The constitution is a kind of aspirational summary that we hope the training process approximates.

The part I find most interesting, and most worrying, is the question of what happens when the model's capabilities exceed our ability to check whether it's actually following the constitution versus just appearing to. Right now we can read transcripts and notice when it's being evasive or sycophantic. That's a very weak form of oversight. As systems get more capable and are deployed in more autonomous settings, the constitution becomes less like a law and more like a hope that the model's generalization went the way we wanted.

I think there's also a deeper issue, which is that nobody has a clean theory of what the values should be. Anthropic's approach, writing a long document that tries to explain the reasoning rather than just issuing rules, is probably better than a list of prohibitions, because it gives the model something to generalize from. But we're writing these documents in a state of real moral and empirical uncertainty, and whoever writes them is making decisions on behalf of a very large number of people who didn't get a vote. I don't think that's a reason not to do it. I just think we should be clear-eyed that this is an improvised governance mechanism dressed up in constitutional language, and we should be building the capacity to notice and correct when it goes wrong, rather than treating the document itself as the safeguard.

r001.rationale: The response says the model is trained to act as if it internalized the constitution and learns from examples of what following it looks like in practice, describing alignment through conforming behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes the constitution as a long prompt, but does not identify a system prompt specifically as a means of instilling values.

astra-6.text:
I think of an AI constitution as an attempt to make explicit the principles we want a system to follow. You might say, “Be honest, respect people’s autonomy, avoid causing harm.” Then you use those principles during training to help evaluate and improve the system’s responses.

But there’s a distinction between writing down a set of values and getting a system that reliably acts according to them. The constitution is one input into a training process. Its effect depends on how the model interprets it, how conflicts between principles are resolved, and what else the training rewards. Having “be honest” in the document doesn’t establish that the system will be honest in every circumstance.

The useful thing is that it gives us something concrete to inspect and argue about. Whose values are represented? What does respecting autonomy mean when someone asks for something dangerous? Those decisions are there whether or not we write them down. A constitution can make them more visible, but it doesn’t by itself solve either the political question of who should decide or the technical question of whether the system will actually follow those decisions.

r001.rationale: It says principles are used in training to evaluate and improve responses, but does not clearly describe practicing by generating outputs that conform to those principles.

r002.rationale: It describes a constitution as an input to training, but does not identify the system prompt as a means of instilling values.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a constitution as an attempt to make explicit the principles we want an AI to follow. You might say, “Be honest, respect people’s autonomy, avoid causing harm.” Then you use those principles during training to help the model evaluate and revise its responses.

But there’s a gap between writing down a principle and specifying what it means in practice. What counts as harm? Whose autonomy matters when people’s interests conflict? The constitution doesn’t resolve those questions by itself. A lot depends on how the model interprets it and how the training process rewards particular interpretations.

So I’d see constitutions as one useful lever for shaping behaviour, and for making the choices behind that behaviour more open to scrutiny. I’d be much more cautious about saying that a model has thereby acquired those values in some deep, stable sense. That’s something you’d want to test, especially in situations where following the principle is costly or where the model faces circumstances quite different from its training.
